rules.quote: For dates in body text, use numerals for the day and year and spell out the name of the month.

rules.violation_condition: An ordinary body-text date has a day or year written in words, an abbreviated month or weekday, or an entirely numeric presentation outside a space-limited context.
when: Use the words-and-numerals form in ordinary content.
Spell out a weekday when it is included.
Spell out the month when the day or year is omitted.
Abbreviated words and numeric dates are allowed when space is limited, including in tables.
Separate conventions apply to data systems and international interchange.
The day-only ordinal exception is handled by the ordinal-date rule.
rules.why: G-2 and G-4: the body-text presentation and the space-limited exceptions are one default-format check, not several findings for the same abbreviated or numeric date.

covers.quote: In Australia, the conventional sequence for dates is ‘day month year’.
Use Australia’s conventional order of ‘day month year’ unless you are writing for users in a country that uses a different style.

rules.quote: Use this sequence when expressing dates in numerals and words.
rules.violation_condition: A date uses a sequence other than day, month, year where the Australian sequence applies.
when: The Australian sequence is day, month, year.
For numeric dates, a different national order is allowed when writing for users in a country that uses it.
ISO interchange dates follow their separate year-first convention.
rules.why: G-2: written and numeric Australian dates share the sequence check, with the stated audience exception.

covers.quote: but don’t include a comma after the day.

rules.quote: Don’t include a comma or any other punctuation.
rules.violation_condition: A date expressed in numerals and words contains internal punctuation, including a comma after the weekday.
when: Applies to the internal structure of a date expressed in numerals and words.
Does not prohibit sentence punctuation following the complete date or an allowed comma between a date and time.
rules.why: G-2: the weekday comma is a case of the same prohibition on punctuation inside a written date.

covers.quote: When you include a year, insert a non-breaking space between the day and month.

rules.quote: Insert a non-breaking space between the day and the month so they stay together on one line.
rules.violation_condition: The day number and written month in a date are not separated by a non-breaking space.
when: Applies to dates with a day number and written month.
Also applies to the dates in a span when a year is included.
rules.why: G-2 and G-4: the later span instruction repeats the same day–month non-breaking-space requirement.

covers.quote: If you refer to the day but not the month, use an ordinal number.

rules.quote: Don’t use an ordinal number (12th, 21st etc.) when writing dates in body text.
rules.violation_condition: A body-text date uses an ordinal day number with a month, or uses a cardinal day number when referring to the day without the month.
when: Use a cardinal day number when the month is included.
Use an ordinal number when referring to the day but not the month.
Determine whether a bare ordinal is a day reference from its sentence.
rules.why: G-2: cardinal versus ordinal day representation changes with the presence of the month.

covers.quote: Don’t use superscript for the ordinal suffix.

rules.quote: Don’t put the ordinal suffix (‘st’, ‘nd’, ‘rd’ or ‘th’) in superscript.
rules.violation_condition: An ordinal suffix in a date or century expression is superscripted.
when: Applies to ordinal day references and ordinal century numbers.
Requires access to formatting or markup; plain-text extraction may lose the distinction.
rules.why: G-2 and G-4: the century instruction repeats the same suffix-formatting check.

covers.quote: Write the years out in full, not as abbreviations.

rules.quote: If you refer to the year only, use the full numerical year. Don’t abbreviate it.
rules.violation_condition: A standalone year reference, or a year in a body-text span expressed with words, is shortened rather than written in full.
when: Applies to year-only references and body-text year spans written with words.
Does not prohibit the separately allowed shortened ending of an en-dash year span.
The restricted two-digit-year convention for numeric dates is a separate case.
The permitted omission in a decade such as ’80s is not a standalone abbreviated year.
rules.why: G-2: the standalone-year and worded-span instructions prohibit the same abbreviated-year form.

covers.quote: Only use the alternatives when the context ensures their meaning is clear.
Only use the shortest form of days and months – ‘F’, ‘M’, ‘N’ and so on – in limited applications.
Only do this if you are sure users will understand what you mean.

rules.quote: Ensure that it is obvious to users which days of the week or months you are referring to.
rules.specification: Assess the abbreviation with its labels, ordering and audience context. The page gives no mechanical threshold for obviousness.
rules.violation_condition: A shortened day or month name cannot be identified unambiguously by the intended users in its context.
when: Alternative weekday abbreviations require context that makes their meaning clear.
The shortest forms, including single capital letters, are restricted to applications where context and order disambiguate them.
Shortened dates in space-limited combined date-and-time displays must also be understandable.
rules.why: G-2: alternative, shortest and display forms are cases of one abbreviation-clarity check.

rules.quote: Don’t use a full stop after shortened days and months.
rules.violation_condition: A shortened day or month name has a full stop marking the abbreviation.
when: A sentence-ending full stop is not an abbreviation full stop.
rules.why: The date-specific instruction produces a checkable finding; its general explanation is not a second rule.

covers.quote: Use a forward slash in numeric dates
This format uses single digits for single-digit days and months.
You can also use 2 digits for each element.

rules.quote: Separate the numbers in a numeric date with an unspaced forward slash, using the format ‘day/month/year’.
rules.violation_condition: An Australian numeric date outside a separately specified technical or interchange format uses a separator other than an unspaced forward slash.
when: Ordinary numeric dates use slashes without surrounding spaces.
The default format uses single digits for single-digit days and months.
Two-digit elements are also permitted.
Computer-application full-stop dates and ISO interchange formats have separate conventions.
The date-order rule handles the audience exception for another country's sequence.
rules.why: G-2 to G-4: consolidate the separator instruction and its format alternatives; two-digit elements are permission, not a ban on leading zeros.

covers.quote: in financial data
if it is clear which century you are referring to
if users understand the order of the elements (‘day month year’ for Australian users).

rules.quote: Only use this style for the year:
rules.violation_condition: A numeric date uses a two-digit year outside financial data, with an unclear century, or for users who do not understand its element order.
when: The restricted style is a two-digit year.
All three stated conditions apply: financial data, a clear century and an understood element order.
Australian users use day, month, year order.
rules.why: G-2: the list supplies the conditions on one two-digit-year check.

rules.quote: Use 2 digits for the day and month and 4 digits for the year: ‘dd.mm.yyyy’.
rules.violation_condition: A full-stop numeric date in a computer-system or application context is not written as dd.mm.yyyy.
when: Applies where a computer system or application uses full stops in numeric dates.
rules.why: G-2: this is the specifically stated computer-application exception to ordinary slash-separated dates.

covers.quote: Don’t use an apostrophe for decades
You can also use an apostrophe to show the missing numerals in a decade

rules.quote: Write decades with an ‘s’ on the end. Don’t use an apostrophe to show the plural.
rules.violation_condition: A numerical decade lacks its plural s or uses an apostrophe to form the plural.
when: An apostrophe may mark omitted leading numerals, as in ’80s.
Casual expressions such as ‘the eighties’ are allowed.
rules.why: G-2 to G-4: decade plural formation is one check, with the omission apostrophe distinguished from a plural apostrophe.

covers.quote: As a general rule, write spans of years in words, using ‘to’, ‘from … to’ or ‘between … and’.
Don’t replace the word between the years with an en dash.
Consider using en dashes for year spans when using words makes the content harder to read.

rules.quote: Use words for spans of years in body text
rules.specification: The named exceptions are actionable; the further exception based on readability needs editorial judgement.
rules.violation_condition: A body-text year span uses an en dash instead of a worded construction where none of the stated en-dash cases applies.
when: Use ‘to’, ‘from … to’ or ‘between … and’ for ordinary body-text year spans.
Exceptions include financial and calendar years, publication and program titles, and parenthesised year spans.
En dashes may also be appropriate where many spans occur or words would make the content harder to read.
rules.why: G-2 and G-4: consolidate the default worded construction and its en-dash exceptions.

covers.quote: Use en dashes for particular types of year spans
financial year
calendar year
span of years in the titles of publications and programs
span of years written in parentheses, such as for a term of office and the years of birth and death.
Always use unspaced en dashes in spans of years. Don’t use forward slashes.

rules.quote: Use an unspaced en dash for a:
rules.violation_condition: A financial-year, calendar-year, title or parenthesised year span is not joined by an unspaced en dash, or another compact year span uses a slash or incorrectly spaced dash.
when: The named cases are financial years, calendar years, year spans in publication and program titles, and year spans in parentheses.
Parenthesised cases include terms of office and birth and death years.
Where an en-dash year span is used in another permitted context, the dash is also unspaced and is not replaced by a forward slash.
rules.why: G-1, G-2 and G-4: the heading and list describe one compact year-span convention; the later slash prohibition restates its separator requirement.

covers.quote: You can also introduce the relevant phrase at first mention and just write the year span, without the phrase, in later mentions.

rules.quote: Always include the phrases ‘financial year’, ‘financial years’, ‘calendar year’ or ‘calendar years’ unless the context makes the meaning clear.
rules.specification: Determining whether context makes the year type clear requires semantic review; do not require the phrase on every occurrence.
rules.violation_condition: A financial-year or calendar-year span is presented without identifying which kind of year it denotes, and the context does not make that meaning clear.
when: The identifying phrase may be introduced at first mention and omitted from later mentions.
The phrase is unnecessary if the meaning is already clear from context.
rules.why: G-2 and G-3: the first-mention option and contextual clarity are exceptions to one identification requirement.

covers.quote: As a general rule, use ‘from … to’ and ‘between … and’ in spans of days and months.
Use en dashes for spans of days and months when space is limited
Only use en dashes for spans of days and months if you have limited space.
But also exercise your judgement – consider using en dashes if using words makes the content harder to read.

rules.quote: Use words for spans of days and months in body text
rules.specification: Space constraints and the exception based on readability require context; no numerical threshold is supplied.
rules.violation_condition: A span of days or months uses an en dash in ordinary body text rather than a worded construction, without a space or readability justification.
when: The general constructions are ‘from … to’ and ‘between … and’.
En dashes are allowed when space is limited, including display text, tables, lists and social media posts.
En dashes may also be used if words would make the content harder to read.
rules.why: G-2 to G-4: worded and en-dash presentations are conditional alternatives, not two checks on the same span.

rules.quote: If it’s appropriate for your content, keep elements of the span together by inserting non-breaking spaces between them.
rules.specification: The page does not define when keeping the whole span together is appropriate. This needs layout or editorial judgement rather than an automatic finding for every span.
rules.violation_condition: A span of days or months that should be kept together for readability contains breakable spaces between its elements.
when: Applies when keeping the span together is appropriate for the content.
The separate day–month non-breaking-space rule still applies to dates within a span.
rules.why: The instruction concerns a property of the text, but its explicit appropriateness condition must not be converted into an unconditional requirement.

covers.quote: The en dash is unspaced when the month only appears at the end of the span.

rules.quote: The en dash is spaced when the day and month appear on both sides of the span.
rules.violation_condition: An en dash in a day-and-month span has the wrong spacing for the elements shown on its two sides.
when: Space the en dash when a day and month appear on both sides.
Do not space it when the month appears only at the end.
rules.why: G-2: spacing changes with the elements present; the prose after the example label states the second case.

covers.quote: Follow the capitalisation of proprietary names.

rules.quote: Use initial capitals for all institutional holidays, religious days and public events.
rules.violation_condition: The name of an institutional holiday, religious day or public event lacks the required initial capitals or departs from its proprietary capitalisation.
when: Follow the capitalisation of proprietary names.
The separate rule for articles and prepositions applies unless proprietary styling overrides it.
rules.why: G-1 and G-2: holidays and events are a specific child check, with proprietary spelling as a condition.

rules.quote: Use lower case for ‘the’ and any prepositions, unless they are capitalised as part of a proprietary name.
rules.violation_condition: An article ‘the’ or a preposition in a named day, public event or historical period is capitalised without a proprietary-name justification.
when: Applies within the names discussed in this section.
Retain capitals that belong to a proprietary name.
Normal sentence-initial capitalisation still applies.
rules.why: G-2: proprietary capitalisation is an exception to one function-word case check.

rules.quote: Use initial capitals for specific periods and events of historical importance, but not when you abbreviate them to a generic term.
rules.violation_condition: A specific historical period or event name is lowercased, or a generic shortened reference to it is capitalised.
when: Distinguish a specific name from a generic reference such as ‘the revolution’ or ‘the battle’.
rules.why: G-2: specific and generic references are conditions on one historical-name capitalisation check.

rules.quote: Use either style, but be consistent in your content.
rules.violation_condition: A document inconsistently alternates between the First/Second World War style and the World War I/II style.
when: The two accepted styles are ‘First World War’ and ‘Second World War’, or ‘World War I’ and ‘World War II’.
Either style is allowed; the check is for consistency.
rules.why: G-3: either style is permitted; only inconsistent use supplies a finding.

rules.quote: Use 2 non-breaking spaces to keep each name together on one line of text.
rules.violation_condition: A full world-war name has breakable spaces between its three components.
when: Applies to the full names in either accepted world-war naming style.
rules.why: This checks the spaces inside a war name, independently of the choice of naming style.

covers.quote: Use a capital ‘i’ – I – for the world wars.
Use roman numerals in the shortened form.
The Style Manual acknowledges that the house styles of some government agencies require the use of the arabic numerals ‘1’ and ‘2’.

rules.quote: Write ‘World War I’ and ‘World War II’ with roman numerals.
rules.violation_condition: A World War I/II name or shortened form uses arabic numerals, lowercase numeral letters or another non-recommended numeral representation.
when: Use capital alphabetic I for the roman numerals.
The same roman-numeral convention applies in shortened forms such as WWI and WWII.
An agency house style requiring arabic 1 and 2 is acknowledged as an exception.
rules.why: G-2 and G-4: full and shortened names share the numeral convention, subject to the acknowledged agency exception.

covers.quote: In content with many mentions of the world wars, you might decide to use a shortened form.

rules.quote: Write the name of the war out in full the first time you use it. Include the shortened form in parentheses immediately afterwards and use the shortened form from then on.
rules.violation_condition: A chosen shortened world-war name is not introduced immediately after the full name in parentheses at first mention, or subsequent references do not use the chosen shortened form.
when: Applies when a shortened form is chosen in content with many mentions of the world wars.
Using a shortened form is optional.
rules.why: G-2 and G-3: introduction and subsequent use form one conditional shortened-name convention.

rules.quote: Use initial capitals for the actual name of a geological era or period but not for broad historical and cultural times.
rules.violation_condition: A geological era or period name is lowercased, or a broad historical or cultural descriptor is capitalised as though it were a specific proper name.
when: Capitalise the actual geological name, not the generic word ‘era’ or ‘period’.
Use lower case for broad historical and cultural descriptors.
rules.why: G-2: geological names and broad cultural descriptors are the contrasting cases of one naming distinction.

rules.quote: Use numerals, not words, for centuries.
rules.violation_condition: A century number is spelled out in words rather than written as an ordinal numeral.
when: Also applies in adjectival compounds such as ‘19th-century’.
rules.why: The century-specific exception is a checkable rule rather than a general ordinal-number restatement.

covers.quote: Write ‘century’ and ‘centuries’ in lower case.

rules.quote: Write ‘century’ and ‘centuries’ in lower case.
rules.violation_condition: The generic word ‘century’ or ‘centuries’ is capitalised within a sentence.
when: Normal sentence-initial capitalisation and proprietary names are not generic mid-sentence uses.
rules.why: G-4: the two occurrences state the same word-case rule.

rules.quote: Don’t use shortened forms, such as 18C or C18, unless you have limited space.
rules.specification: The space-limited exception needs layout or content-context information.
rules.violation_condition: A century is expressed in a shortened form such as 18C or C18 where space is not limited.
when: Shortened century forms are allowed when space is limited.
rules.why: G-2 and G-3: the space-limited permission qualifies one shortened-century check.

rules.quote: Use CE and BCE to represent the common era (CE) and the time before the common era (BCE).
rules.violation_condition: An era designation uses an alternative to CE or BCE for the common era or the time before it.
when: Applies when an era designation is supplied; the sentence does not require one on every year.
rules.why: The instruction chooses era designations; the following chronology explanation is not an additional instruction.

rules.quote: Write ‘CE’ and ‘BCE’ without full stops
rules.violation_condition: The CE or BCE era designation contains abbreviation full stops.
rules.why: The punctuation property is independently flaggable from the following spacing requirement.

rules.quote: Write ‘CE’ and ‘BCE’ without full stops and with a non-breaking space separating them from the year or century.
rules.violation_condition: A CE or BCE designation is not separated from its year or century by a non-breaking space.
when: This item checks the spacing clause only; full stops are checked separately.
rules.why: One sentence states two independent properties; this rule checks the required separator.

covers.quote: In body text, use lower case for generic terms like the names of seasons –‘autumn’ – and astronomical events such as ‘equinox’ and ‘solstice’.

rules.quote: Use lower case for the seasons and recurrent seasonal events.
rules.violation_condition: A generic season, recurrent seasonal event or astronomical event name is capitalised in body text.
when: Includes generic references such as autumn, equinox and solstice.
Normal sentence-initial capitals and actual proper names are not violations.
rules.why: G-2 and G-4: the introductory instruction and seasonal subsection specify the same generic-term case convention.

covers.quote: Write times of day using numerals, especially when you need to convey precise times.
In these situations, use numerals and the word ‘o’clock’.

rules.quote: Use numerals for times of day
rules.violation_condition: An ordinary time-of-day expression spells out its numerical time components in words.
when: Particularly applies when precise times must be conveyed.
Noon, midday and midnight are the prescribed word forms for those times.
When ‘o’clock’ is allowed in a quotation or transcription, its hour is still written as a numeral.
rules.why: G-2 and G-4: the body restates the heading; the o’clock case retains the same numeral requirement.

covers.quote: Use a colon to separate the hours, minutes and seconds in the 24-hour clock.
Some government agencies that produce technical and scientific content don’t use a colon for the 24-hour clock – for example, 2300 and 0430.
If space is limited and you use the 24-hour clock in general content, we recommend inserting a colon for clarity.
The numbers can be unspaced (basic format) or separated by a colon (extended format).

rules.quote: Use a colon between the hours and minutes.
rules.violation_condition: A time expression uses a non-colon separator between hours and minutes, or between minutes and included seconds in a 24-hour time, outside an allowed basic-format context.
when: Use colons for ordinary time expressions and extended 24-hour times.
Technical and scientific agency content may use separator-free basic 24-hour format.
Basic-format international interchange times may omit separators.
A colon is recommended for clarity when a 24-hour time is used in space-limited general content.
rules.why: G-2 and G-4: consolidate time-separator instructions and retain the technical and ISO basic-format exceptions.

rules.quote: Write ‘am’ and ‘pm’ in lower case.
rules.violation_condition: A time-of-day initialism am or pm is written with capital letters.
when: Applies when the letters designate a time of day, not another meaning of AM or PM.
rules.why: Letter case is an independent property from the following non-breaking-space instruction.

rules.quote: Separate the numbers and the initialism with a non-breaking space.
rules.violation_condition: A time number and its am or pm designation are not separated by a non-breaking space.
when: Applies to 12-hour times with am or pm.
rules.why: This checks the required separator rather than the independent case of am or pm.

rules.quote: Don’t use ‘am’ and ‘pm’ with words that duplicate their meaning, for example ‘morning’ and ‘afternoon’.
rules.violation_condition: A time expression combines am or pm with a redundant word or phrase identifying the same part of the day.
when: The word or phrase must duplicate the meaning of the time's am or pm designation.
rules.why: The nearest instruction tests redundancy, not the general formatting of the times in its examples.

rules.quote: Use ‘noon’, ‘midday’ or ‘midnight’ instead of ‘12 am’ or ‘12 pm’.
rules.violation_condition: Noon or midnight is expressed as 12 am or 12 pm rather than noon, midday or midnight.
when: Does not replace non-zero minute expressions such as 12:30 pm.
The separate 24-hour-clock convention remains available.
rules.why: The body states the actionable preference; the heading only names the topic.

rules.quote: Write ‘o’clock’ only when you quote someone directly or transcribe a recording.
rules.violation_condition: The word ‘o’clock’ appears in an original time expression rather than a direct quotation or transcription.
when: Direct quotations and recording transcriptions may use ‘o’clock’.
rules.why: G-2 and G-3: quotation and transcription are exceptions to the use restriction; numeral representation is checked separately.

covers.quote: travel
certain scientific fields
the armed services
content written for countries using the 24-hour clock.

rules.quote: Use the 24-hour clock if it helps people understand your content.
rules.specification: Audience benefit must be established; the listed contexts are indicators, not an unconditional ban on 12-hour times.
rules.violation_condition: A 12-hour presentation makes a time harder for the intended audience to understand where a 24-hour presentation would resolve that problem.
when: Particularly relevant to travel, certain scientific fields, the armed services and audiences in countries using the 24-hour clock.
Limited space can also make the 24-hour clock useful.
rules.why: G-2: the list changes when this audience-dependent format recommendation applies.

covers.quote: It can have 6 digits if seconds are included:
The first 2 digits are the hours.
The next 2 digits are the minutes.
The last 2 digits are the seconds, if you include them.
Always use a ‘leading zero’ for hours under 10 – for example, write ‘05:30’ not ‘5:30’.
followed by 2-digit numbers for the hour, minute and second.

rules.quote: It always uses at least 4 digits.
rules.violation_condition: A 24-hour time does not contain two-digit hour and minute components, or has a seconds component that is not two digits.
when: A 24-hour time has HHMM components, with optional SS.
Hours below 10 require a leading zero.
Separators are governed by the separate time-separator rule.
Also applies to the numeric components of ISO local-time representations.
rules.why: G-2 and G-4: leading zeros and two-digit components are cases of the same fixed-width 24-hour representation.

rules.quote: Don’t add ‘am’ or ‘pm’ to times written in 24-hour clock format.
rules.violation_condition: A time written in 24-hour format has an am or pm designation.
when: Distinguish a 24-hour time from an ordinary 12-hour time before flagging.
rules.why: This is a separate incompatibility check, not a restatement of numeric width or separators.

rules.quote: Write the initialism ‘UTC’, followed by ‘+’ or ‘−’, followed by the time offset to UTC in 24-hour system format.
rules.violation_condition: A written UTC offset does not have UTC followed by a plus or minus sign and the offset in 24-hour system format.
when: Applies when expressing a time zone as an offset to UTC.
The examples use UTC+HH:MM and UTC−HH:MM.
rules.why: The body gives the actionable offset syntax; the surrounding paragraphs explain UTC.

covers.quote: Use en dashes for spans of time when space is limited
But also exercise your judgement – consider using en dashes if using words makes the content harder to read.

rules.quote: Only use en dashes for time spans if you have limited space.
rules.specification: Space constraints and comparative readability require context; do not infer them from a made-up character limit.
rules.violation_condition: A time span uses an en dash without a space constraint or the stated readability justification.
when: Limited-space contexts can include display text, tables, lists and social media posts.
An en dash may also be used if words would make the content harder to read.
rules.why: G-2 to G-4: the body limits the heading, with an explicit readability exception.

covers.quote: if the ‘am’ or ‘pm’ appears only at the end of the span
for spans of time in the 24-hour clock format.
Use a spaced en dash:
when ‘am’ or ‘pm’ appears on both sides of the span
if ‘noon’, ‘midday’ or ‘midnight’ appears in the span.

rules.quote: Use an unspaced en dash:
rules.violation_condition: An en dash in a time span is spaced or unspaced contrary to the elements present on its two sides.
when: Use an unspaced dash when am or pm occurs only at the end.
Use an unspaced dash for 24-hour-clock spans.
Use a spaced dash when am or pm occurs on both sides.
Use a spaced dash when noon, midday or midnight occurs in the span.
rules.why: G-2: these are four conditions on one time-span dash-spacing check.

rules.quote: Don’t combine words and the en dash.
rules.violation_condition: A time-span construction combines a range word such as ‘between’ or ‘from’ with an en dash in place of its matching word.
when: Applies to mixed range constructions, not all words appearing near a dashed time span.
rules.why: E-2: the nearby contrast tests mixed range syntax, independently of dash spacing.

covers.quote: Spell out the units of time: ‘hours’, ‘minutes’ and ‘seconds’.
Use shortened forms for units of time when space is limited
It is usually better to spell out the units that measure time.

rules.quote: Only use short forms if space is limited and the short forms are easy to identify correctly.
rules.specification: Space limitation and audience recognition need context. In ordinary body text, spell out the units.
rules.violation_condition: A duration uses a shortened time unit where space is not limited or the shortened unit cannot be identified correctly.
when: The default is to spell out units such as hours, minutes and seconds.
Short forms require both limited space and correct identification.
Data systems may require system-specific forms.
rules.why: G-2 to G-4: spelling out units is the default, and limited space plus clarity supplies the exception.

rules.quote: Use fractions written in words if users only need a general idea of values.
rules.specification: The trigger is the audience's need for approximate rather than precise information; the page supplies no numerical precision threshold.
rules.violation_condition: A duration intended to give only a general idea of its value uses a numerical fraction rather than a fraction written in words.
when: Applies to duration fractions where users need only a general idea.
Does not require every duration to be converted into a fraction.
rules.why: G-2: the audience's precision needs limit the worded-fraction instruction.

covers.quote: Only use decimal numbers if they are the best way to explain what people need to know.

rules.quote: It is usually better to avoid decimals and include the number and unit of time.
rules.specification: This is a clarity preference, not a blanket prohibition on decimal durations. Whether a decimal is the best explanation depends on audience and purpose.
rules.violation_condition: A duration is expressed as a decimal where explicit numbers and time units would communicate the value more clearly.
when: Decimal durations are allowed when they are the best way to explain what people need to know.
Do not mistake a decimal fraction of an hour for a number of minutes.
Precise decimal seconds may be appropriate.
rules.why: G-2 and G-4: the restriction and preference describe one decimal-versus-explicit-units clarity check.

covers.quote: second – s
minute – min
hour – h
day – d
week – wk
month – mo
year – y or yr
Data systems support specific (and usually several) shortened forms for units of time.

rules.quote: If you need to abbreviate time, use the following units as shortened forms:
rules.violation_condition: A shortened time unit uses a form other than the listed forms for its unit.
when: The listed forms are s, min, h, d, wk, mo, and y or yr.
Data systems may support or require other forms according to their specifications.
rules.why: G-2: the list supplies the values for one shortened-unit lookup check, with a system-specific exception.

rules.quote: Choose one and use it consistently in your document.
rules.violation_condition: A document inconsistently uses both y and yr as the shortened form for year.
when: Either y or yr is permitted.
Applies when using shortened forms for the unit year.
